cues.text: Centuries of Growing Estrangement
The rupture of 1054 was less a single event than the visible eruption of tensions accumulating between Constantinople and Rome for centuries.

These included disputes over the papacy's authority relative to the other patriarchs, disagreements over the filioque clause added to the Nicene Creed in the West, differing customs such as clerical celibacy, and simmering resentment over Rome's claims to universal jurisdiction.
Michael Cerularius and the Immediate Dispute

In 1053, Michael Cerularius , Patriarch of Constantinople, ordered the closure of Latin-rite churches in the city and had their tabernacles trampled after Norman rulers in southern Italy compelled Greek churches there to adopt unleavened bread for the Eucharist.
Cerularius also had an ally, Archbishop Leo of Ohrid, circulate a letter sharply attacking Latin liturgical customs, particularly the use of unleavened bread, as quasi-Judaizing errors.
The Legation of Cardinal Humbert
Pope Leo IX dispatched a delegation to Constantinople led by the combative Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida to resolve the dispute.

Negotiations went badly: Cerularius refused further dealings with the legates, and on July 16, 1054 , during the Divine Liturgy at Hagia Sophia, Humbert strode to the altar and laid down a bull of excommunication against Cerularius and his associates.
Pope Leo IX had, in fact, already died some weeks earlier, a detail that has led some historians to question the technical validity of the act.
Mutual Excommunication
Cerularius responded within days by convening a synod that excommunicated Humbert and his fellow legates in turn.

At the time, neither side clearly intended a permanent, general schism between the whole Eastern and Western Churches — the excommunications named only individuals — but the estrangement, once begun, was never healed.
How a Local Quarrel Became a Permanent Division
What made 1054 decisive was not the excommunications themselves but their aftermath.
One by one, the other Eastern patriarchates followed Cerularius's lead.

Out of long habit of deferring to Constantinople, they struck the pope's name from their own diptychs, gradually transforming a personal dispute into a lasting rift between Latin West and Byzantine East.
Attempts at reunion at the Second Council of Lyons (1274) and the Council of Florence (1439) achieved formal but short-lived reconciliations.
Legacy
The Great Schism remains the deepest and most enduring division within historic Christendom, separating the Catholic Church from what became the Eastern Orthodox communion.
It reshaped Europe's religious map for the remainder of the Middle Ages and deepened mutual suspicion during the Crusades.
This was most disastrous in the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople in 1204.
Despite modern dialogue efforts and the mutual lifting of the 1054 excommunications by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras in 1965, it remains formally unresolved to this day.
